title: Intermediate Legs HIIT: 8 Bodyweight Exercises for Fat Burn
description: A 40-minute intermediate HIIT session focused entirely on the lower body. Eight high-intensity bodyweight exercises that torch calories, build leg endurance, and leave your quads, glutes and hamstrings genuinely worked.
text:
Lower body HIIT is the most metabolically demanding form of interval training available without equipment. The legs contain the largest muscle groups in the body: the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes together account for roughly 40% of total muscle mass. Training them at high intensity creates a disproportionately large cardiovascular and metabolic response compared to upper-body-focused or full-body sessions of equal duration. For fat loss specifically, this makes leg-focused HIIT one of the highest-return training choices per unit of time.

This 40-minute intermediate session uses a 40:20 interval structure throughout: 40 seconds of maximum sustainable effort, 20 seconds of transition and rest. At the intermediate level, this ratio keeps work density high enough to maintain heart rate in the 75-85% maximum range across the full session, which is the zone where fat oxidation and cardiovascular adaptation are both optimized simultaneously.

The eight exercises are organized in a deliberate sequence. Bilateral movements come first when the legs are fresh and can produce maximum force output. Unilateral variations follow to address left-right strength asymmetries and increase the stabilization demand per leg. Plyometric exercises are placed after the bilateral and unilateral strength work, when the muscles are pre-loaded with fatigue that forces maximum motor unit recruitment during the explosive phases. Isometric holds close the session when glycogen is depleted and the muscles must sustain tension without the benefit of the stretch-shortening cycle.

For intermediate athletes, the key distinction from a beginner leg HIIT session is the expectation of intent. Every work interval should be performed at a pace that makes completing a full conversation difficult. If you reach the 20-second rest feeling like you could have worked harder, your intensity was insufficient to produce the EPOC response that drives post-workout fat burn for 18-24 hours after the session ends.

Progression over time follows three paths: increasing the work interval from 40 to 45 to 50 seconds while holding rest at 20, adding a fourth round of the full circuit, or advancing to weighted variations of the same movements using dumbbells or a loaded backpack once bodyweight output becomes insufficient to maintain target heart rate.

Train this program twice per week with at least 48 hours between sessions. Pairing it with an upper body session on alternate days produces a complete weekly training structure without redundant lower body loading that would compromise recovery. Expect meaningful improvements in leg endurance, definition, and fat loss within 6-8 weeks of consistent application.
targetMuscleGroups: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Gluteus Medius, Hamstrings, Calves, Core

nutritionAdvice.preWorkout: Eat a moderate meal 75-90 minutes before this session. Target 45-60g of complex carbohydrates and 25-30g of lean protein: brown rice with chicken breast, oatmeal with a scoop of protein powder and banana, or whole grain toast with eggs. Lower body HIIT at intermediate intensity depletes leg glycogen rapidly, and training with insufficient carbohydrate stores produces noticeably reduced power output on the plyometric intervals. Avoid high-fat meals in the 90 minutes before training: fat slows gastric emptying and causes discomfort during squat-pattern movements that compress the abdomen.
nutritionAdvice.postWorkout: Within 45 minutes of finishing, consume 25-35g of protein and 50-65g of moderate-glycemic carbohydrates to initiate muscle protein synthesis and replenish depleted leg glycogen. Greek yogurt with granola and honey, a protein shake with oat milk and a banana, or a meal of rice with lean protein are all well-matched to the session demand. Despite the fat-loss goal, do not aggressively restrict calories in this meal: the leg muscles undergo significant mechanical stress during this session and require adequate substrate to repair and maintain the lean tissue that sustains your resting metabolic rate.
nutritionAdvice.hydration: Drink 500ml of water in the 60-90 minutes before training. During the 40-minute session, drink 200-250ml every 12-15 minutes, drinking during the 20-second rest intervals rather than interrupting work intervals. After training, drink at least 600ml within 30 minutes. Leg HIIT at intermediate intensity produces significant sweat volume, and even 1.5% dehydration measurably reduces lower body power output and the coordination required for safe landing mechanics during jump exercises. In warm conditions or summer training, add an electrolyte supplement to your intra-workout water.

exercises.name: Sumo Squat Pulse
exercises.technique: Stand with feet wider than shoulder width and toes pointing out at 45 degrees. Lower into a sumo squat until your thighs reach parallel to the floor. Hold this bottom position throughout the entire interval. From the parallel position, pulse upward 8-10 cm and return to the bottom continuously, keeping tension in the quads, glutes, and inner thighs at all times. Your heels stay flat on the floor throughout. Keep your chest upright and your knees pushed outward in line with your toes for the full 40 seconds. The pulse range is small and deliberate: larger ranges reduce time under tension and allow the muscles to rest at the top. At the end of the interval, stand to complete the set.
exercises.tips: The sumo pulse is a constant-tension exercise: the muscles never reach a point of relief during the interval. This sustained isometric plus small dynamic contraction creates a high degree of metabolic stress in the quads and adductors, which drives both the burning sensation and the fat-burning hormonal response. Keep pushing your knees outward throughout the interval; they will want to cave inward as fatigue builds.
exercises.commonMistakes: Standing too high between pulses and releasing tension from the legs, which turns the exercise into intermittent partial squats rather than sustained lower-body loading. Allowing the knees to cave inward as quad fatigue accumulates. Leaning the torso forward rather than maintaining an upright chest throughout the hold.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Adductors, Gluteus Maximus, Gluteus Medius, Calves

exercises.name: Alternating Reverse Lunge
exercises.technique: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step backward with your right foot, landing on the ball of that foot. Lower your back knee toward the floor until both knees reach approximately 90 degrees: front shin vertical, front thigh parallel to the floor. Drive through your front heel to return to standing, bringing your right foot back to the starting position. Immediately step backward with your left foot and repeat. Alternate legs continuously for the full 40 seconds. Keep your torso upright throughout: resist the lean forward as fatigue accumulates. Each rep should be controlled on the way down and powerful on the drive back to standing.
exercises.tips: At intermediate level, add a brief 1-second pause at the bottom of each rep to eliminate the elastic rebound from the reversal and force the quad and glute to generate force from a momentary dead stop. This doubles the difficulty without adding complexity or equipment. Drive from the front heel rather than pushing off the back foot: heel drive maximizes glute activation on the working leg.
exercises.commonMistakes: Stepping too short, causing the front knee to travel well past the toes. Letting the front knee cave inward on the drive back to standing. Using a fast bouncy tempo that uses momentum rather than muscular effort to complete each rep.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Hip Flexors, Core

exercises.name: Lateral Lunge to Curtsy
exercises.technique: Stand with feet together. Step your right foot directly to the right into a lateral lunge: bend your right knee, push your hips back and to the right, keep your left leg straight. Descend until your right thigh approaches parallel. From the lateral lunge position, drive back to standing and immediately step your right foot behind and across your left leg into a curtsy lunge: lower your right knee toward the floor behind your left foot while keeping your left knee tracking over your left toes. Drive back to standing. That full sequence, lateral lunge plus curtsy, is one rep. Complete all reps on the right side for the first interval, switch to the left for the second.
exercises.tips: This combination targets the gluteus medius through the lateral lunge and the gluteus maximus through the curtsy in a single continuous movement, making it one of the most complete glute-focused exercises in a bodyweight lower body circuit. Keep your chest upright throughout both movements and drive from the working heel on every return to standing.
exercises.commonMistakes: Allowing the knee of the lateral lunge to cave inward rather than tracking over the toes. Crossing the curtsy foot too close to the standing foot, which reduces balance and limits the depth available. Rushing the transition between the two movements and losing positional control.
exercises.muscles: Gluteus Medius, Gluteus Maximus, Adductors, Quadriceps, Hamstrings, Core

exercises.name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
exercises.technique: Stand on your left foot with a soft bend in the knee. Hinge forward at the hip by pushing your hips backward while simultaneously extending your right leg behind you, keeping it in line with your torso. Lower your torso toward the floor until it reaches approximately parallel: your right leg extends behind you and your arms reach toward the floor or forward for balance. Keep your back completely flat throughout. Drive your left hip forward and squeeze your left glute to return to standing, bringing your right leg back under your body. Complete all reps on the left leg, then switch. The movement is slow and controlled: 2 seconds down, 1 second pause at parallel, 2 seconds back up.
exercises.tips: A slight bend in the standing knee is correct and protective: do not lock the knee straight. For balance, focus on a fixed point on the floor approximately 1 meter in front of you. If balance is consistently breaking down, hold one fingertip lightly against a wall on the non-working side: the fingertip contact provides proprioceptive stability without offloading the balance challenge entirely.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rotating the hip of the raised leg outward so the foot points sideways rather than straight down, which reduces hamstring engagement and creates a hip rotation pattern rather than a hinge. Rounding the lower back to increase range of motion rather than stopping at neutral spine. Locking the standing knee straight, which increases hamstring tension beyond a safe level and reduces the glute involvement.
exercises.muscles: Hamstrings, Gluteus Maximus, Erector Spinae, Adductor Magnus, Core

exercises.name: Jump Squat
exercises.technique: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Lower into a full squat with a 2-second controlled descent until thighs reach parallel. From the bottom, drive explosively through your entire foot and extend hips, knees, and ankles simultaneously to jump vertically. Reach arms overhead at peak height to maximize jump height. Land with feet in their original position, absorbing the impact over 2 full seconds through bent ankles, knees, and hips before transitioning directly into the next squat descent. The landing and the descent into the next rep form one continuous controlled movement. Every concentric should be performed at maximum explosive intent regardless of fatigue.
exercises.tips: Jump height is the metric of quality in this exercise: if your jumps are getting significantly lower as the interval progresses, your intensity in the early reps was too high. Aim for consistent height across all reps rather than maximum height on the first few followed by barely leaving the floor. Quiet landings through soft joint absorption protect the knees and train the deceleration mechanics that prevent injury in all jumping activities.
exercises.commonMistakes: Landing with straight or minimally bent knees, which transfers full impact force to the joint. Allowing knees to cave inward on both the squat descent and the landing. Using a shallow quarter-squat depth to make the jump easier, which significantly reduces quad and glute involvement.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Calves, Core

exercises.name: Lateral Bound
exercises.technique: Stand on your right foot with your knee slightly bent and hips in a quarter-squat position. Drive explosively off your right foot to jump laterally to the left, covering as much horizontal distance as possible. Land on your left foot only, absorbing the landing through a bent knee and hip in a single-leg squat position. Pause for one full second to stabilize on the left foot before driving explosively back to the right. Each bound is a maximal lateral jump landing on a single leg with a controlled, stable landing. Alternate continuously for the full 40 seconds. Swing your arms in the direction of travel to generate momentum and improve jump distance.
exercises.tips: The lateral bound is one of the most effective fat-burning leg exercises in bodyweight HIIT because it combines maximum power output with a demanding single-leg landing that requires simultaneous strength, balance, and deceleration. The 1-second landing pause is the technical priority: stick every landing before bounding back. If landings are unstable, reduce the jump distance until single-leg landing mechanics are solid.
exercises.commonMistakes: Landing with a straight knee rather than absorbing through a bent knee and hip, which sends impact force into the joint. Skipping the 1-second landing pause and rebounding immediately using elastic energy rather than true muscular control. Allowing the landing knee to cave inward rather than tracking over the toes.
exercises.muscles: Gluteus Maximus, Gluteus Medius, Quadriceps, Hamstrings, Calves, Core

exercises.name: Glute Bridge March
exercises.technique: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Drive through both heels and lift your hips into a glute bridge, squeezing your glutes hard at the top. Hold the bridge position throughout the interval. From the bridged position, lift your right knee toward your chest, keeping your hips completely level and your left heel driving into the floor. Lower the right foot back to the floor and immediately lift the left knee. Alternate legs in a slow, controlled marching pattern for the full 40 seconds without dropping your hips. Each knee lift should take 2 seconds up and 2 seconds down.
exercises.tips: The hip bridge hold during the march creates continuous isometric glute loading on the standing leg while the marching leg works dynamically. This combination produces significantly higher glute activation than a standard bridge or a bodyweight march performed separately. The key is maintaining hip level throughout: if your hips drop on one side when you lift the opposite knee, you are losing the isometric glute contraction that makes the exercise effective.
exercises.commonMistakes: Dropping the hips between leg lifts rather than maintaining the full bridge height throughout the interval. Lifting the knee so high that the lower back arches to compensate. Rushing the march and losing hip stability, which turns the exercise into a momentum drill rather than a controlled glute isolation movement.
exercises.muscles: Gluteus Maximus, Gluteus Medius, Hamstrings, Core, Hip Flexors

exercises.name: Wall Sit with Heel Raise
exercises.technique: Stand with your back against a wall and slide down until your thighs are parallel to the floor and your knees are at 90 degrees directly over your ankles. Press your entire back flat against the wall. Hold this position throughout the full interval. Every 5 seconds, raise both heels off the floor simultaneously by pressing through the balls of your feet, contracting the calves at the peak, then lower them back to the floor. Continue alternating between full flat-foot wall sit and heel-raised wall sit for the full 40 seconds. Your thighs must stay parallel throughout: do not let the hips rise higher than the knee line to make the heel raises easier.
exercises.tips: The wall sit is one of the highest time-under-tension quad exercises available in bodyweight training, and adding the heel raise incorporates the calves into an already demanding isometric hold. By the final 10 seconds of the interval the quads will be burning significantly: this metabolic stress is the intended stimulus. Keep pressing your back firmly into the wall to prevent the hips from sliding up as fatigue accumulates.
exercises.commonMistakes: Allowing the hips to rise above knee level as fatigue builds, which reduces quad engagement and makes the position easier. Letting the knees drift forward past the toes, which increases patellar stress. Performing the heel raises with a reduced range of motion rather than a full calf contraction at the top.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gastrocnemius, Soleus, Gluteus Maximus, Core
